Abstract 
The synergistic development of nanophotonics and machine learning has inspired tremendous innovations 
in both fields in the past decade. In diverse photonics research, deep-learning methods using artificial neural 
networks become the key game changer that greatly facilitates rapid nanophotonics design and the versatile 
processing of optical information. Moreover, optical computing platforms that perform calculations through light 
propagation are receiving tremendous interest as next-generation machine-learning hardware with advantages 
in computing speed, energy efficiency, and parallelism. This review summarizes the current state-of-the-art 
nanophotonic devices enabled by machine learning and analyzes the longstanding challenges that must 
be overcome to make an impact on technology. We also discuss the opportunities of intelligent photonics 
in applications such as computational imaging/sensing and machine vision. The intersection of nanophotonics 
with deep learning holds tremendous implications for transformative technologies ranging from internet of things 
to smart health. Lastly, we provide our perspective on the pressing challenges in intelligent photonics that must be 
tackled to advance this field to the next level and the vast opportunities for multidisciplinary collaboration.
1  Introduction
Visual information plays a key role in human activity for 
understanding our surrounding environments. Similarly, 
the ability to collect and analyze optical information is 
essential for artificial intelligence (AI) systems developed 
to replace human intelligence. From object recognition 
to pattern analysis (e.g. medical diagnostics) and real-
time decision making (e.g. autonomous driving), the 
collaboration between optical elements and computing 
platforms has been the core of these technologies [1, 2]. 
Despite these successes, the machine vision components 
of the AI systems still face challenges that can prevent 
them from large-scale deployment in next-generation 
intelligent platforms. In general, the major mission 
of AI technology is to replace the role of humans in 
repetitive, labor-intensive tasks with machine power 
to promote better productivity. Therefore, the focus of 
AI technology must shift from large-scale, centralized 
servers towards a ubiquitous-computing scheme, where

Figure  1 shows a timeline of major breakthroughs in

The performance of ANNs improved considerably, from

[23, 24].
Photonics undergoes a paradigm shift towards

The grand convergence of nanophotonics and machine 
learning has become extremely compelling in the past 
decade (Fig. 2a). Initially, machine learning contributed 
to areas including inverse photonics design [33–36], 
computational microscopy [37]/sensing [38, 39], and 
metrology [40]. Then, photonic neural networks [41–
43]—physical machine-learning systems implemented by 
light propagation and light-matter interaction—started 
to emerge with advantages over their electronic coun-
terparts including processing speed and energy con-
sumption [44–47], which are becoming serious issues as 
models grow in scale. As optical devices, their ability to 
simultaneously process free-space information provides 
unprecedented opportunities for building intelligent edge 
devices with sensing-computing integration. For usage in 
diverse real-world applications, however, optical neural 
networks still need tremendous improvement in their key 
performance including accuracy and generalizability. The 
ability to reprogram during operation is also critical for 
AI-driven applications but is often lacking in these intel-
ligent optical processors. Additionally, fabrication chal-
lenges are preventing the integration of optical machine 
learning systems with electronics as high-speed proces-
sors. Figure 2b, c further justifies the trends of intelligent 
photonics by surveying the number of relevant publica-
tions on topics including ANNs, metasurface, on-chip 
neural networks, and diffractive neural networks. While 
continuing to receive tremendous attention, the rapid 
growth in the ANN model size [12, 13, 48–53] (as shown 
in Fig.  2c) in the past decade motivates the invention 
of optical neural networks [44, 45, 54–56] to tackle the 
upcoming bottleneck in speed and energy efficiency.
This review aims to discuss the opportunities 
enabled by intelligent photonics at the intersection of 
nanophotonics and deep learning and their impact on

2.1  Intelligent free‑space optical processors
All-optical machine learning is first realized in free 
space by successive phase-modulation layers with learn-
able transmittance parameters similar to the bias terms 
in digital ANNs (Fig.  3a) [45]. The networks are opti-
mized via a deep-learning-training process and the fab-
ricated designs can perform machine learning tasks such 
as inference and machine vision [57, 58] within a single 
pass of light propagation. For example, phase-retrieval 
is a long-standing challenge in imaging and holography 
because common detectors only sense intensity. As free-
space devices, diffractive layers can directly sense spatial 
phase distributions from imaging targets and convert 
this information into intensity distributions at the output

complex field modulation [74, 75] (Fig. 3c).

Therefore, metasurfaces that can tailor polarization [77], 
spectral [31, 78, 79], and temporal properties [80] of 
light at subwavelength scale have tremendous potential 
in capturing multidimensional optical information. Full 
utilization of multiple optical degrees of freedom by a 
single metasurface is typically realized by direct spatial 
multiplexing [81] or analytic solutions [82] based on 
wave-optics that lack flexibility. The deep-learning-
based design framework of diffractive networks thereby 
provides a transformative design strategy for the efficient 
design of these metasurface devices.
For centralized computing, diffractive and metasurface 
networks currently exhibit limited competitiveness 
but are highly promising in building fast, large-scale 
AI models with low power consumption. Compared to 
integrated photonics [44], free-space optical networks 
have larger freedom in neural connectivity because 
of their extra dimensionality for light propagation. 
However, the lack of effective training strategy similar 
to residual learning [11] is hindering the realization 
of depth advantage, which is critical for sophisticated 
tasks. One promising strategy to accelerate the training 
of diffractive networks is in-situ learning [83, 84] based 
on experimental optical systems that compute the 
forward model optically, with near-zero latency and 
minimum power consumption (Fig.  3e). By leveraging 
reciprocity, on-site optimization can be significantly 
accelerated using a back-propagation-free process that 
eliminates the time-consuming calculations of gradients 
[85]. However, they are only demonstrated by systems 
that allow dynamic tuning of all trainable diffractive 
neurons. For example, although such training can be 
performed on visible-light spatial light modulators, 
their large pixel sizes and thicknesses preclude compact 
network designs, e.g. subwavelength neurons and short 
layer-to-layer distances, which are more suitable for 
on-chip integration. Fortunately, diffractive networks 
are wavelength-scalable, where the same design can 
operate at arbitrary wavelengths by physically expanding 
or shrinking the network features in proportion to the 
operation wavelengths. Therefore, architectures that 
cannot be implemented by existing tunable devices can 
possibly be designed at a different wavelength by training 
a physically scaled equivalence with accessible hardware. 
Lastly, further adoption of physics-informed [86, 87] 
frameworks that utilize principles of light propagation 
and light-matter interactions can accelerate the training 
of free-space optical networks.
The implementation of nonlinear activation functions 
is also a long-standing challenge for optical computing 
because of the low efficiency of nonlinear optical 
processes [88–90], significantly degrading their energy 
efficiency. For example, lasing actions from coherent 
nanolaser arrays can potentially serve as a nonlinear

2.2  Integrated optical computing systems
Photonic integrated circuits (PICs) are another impor-
tant class of architectures that operate on photons within 
planar chips to perform optical computing [97] and infor-
mation processing [98]. As building blocks of PICs, Si 
waveguides realized extraordinarily low losses (~ 0.3 dB/
cm) [99, 100] that makes light propagation on chip fast 
and efficient [101] (Fig.  4a). Materials innovations on 
­Si3N4 [102] and ­LiNbO3 [103] further achieved lower 
losses across broad wavelengths range and electro-opti-
cal/nonlinear modulation, respectively [101–104]. Wave-
guides enable high-performance computing systems that 
require high-throughput, immediate communication 
between individual processing units at minimum energy 
consumption. In particular, Intel showcased a chiplet 
using optical interconnects that realized ~ 4 terabits/s 
data transfer rate at 5 pJ/bit [105]. TSMC also demon-
strated a digital optical chip using ­Si3N4 waveguides and 
photodetectors which could perform massive matrix 
math (up to 4096 × 4096) with a low power consump-
tion of < 0.2 pJ/bit [106]. Other on-chip units including 
transceivers [107–109] and photonic switches [110, 111] 
to frequency filters [112] are also crucial for interactive 
synchronization between intelligent devices.
Machine learning in PICs [44] were developed using 
Mach–Zehnder interferometers (MZIs) that consist 
of two parallel waveguides, where the interference-
tuned outputs are controlled by their path differences 
using thermo-optic phase shifters (Fig.  4b) [113].

Micro-ring resonators [117] also play a key role 
in optical computing systems with programmable 
transmission coefficient that can be used to implement 
the weights of the photonic neural networks [118]. 
Initially, these on-chip units are used as wavelengths-
selective filters that can be used for wavelength division 
multiplexing [119] and optical switching [120]. By 
tuning the weights of micro-ring resonator arrays via 
heating, these photonic chips perform machine learning 
tasks ranging from fiber nonlinearity compensation 
[121], signal classification [122], and spatial–temporal 
recognition [123]. Collaboration with other on-chip 
computing units such as MZIs has also been reported 
where the micro-ring units serve as multi-wavelength 
processors while MZIs can perform pre-encoding of 
input information [124].
On-chip diffractive networks [125] are additional 
powerful processors for performing operations such 
as convolution [126] and Fourier transform via light 
propagation (Fig.  4c) [127]. Addition of diffractive 
cells can reduce the number of MZI units needed for 
performing matric operations as well as the overall 
energy consumption. Importantly, a scaled-up photonic 
neural network has been realized by a chiplet-based 
architecture where each unit consists of (1) planar 
diffraction-based encoders/decoders as the compressor/
decompressor for input/output data; and (2) MZI 
arrays that serve as effective feature embeddings. For 
image recognition, pixels in a large image are divided 
into patches, sent to chiplets via diffractive encoders, 
sequentially processed by multiple chiplets, and then 
combined to generate the output, achieving an overall 
accuracy comparable to the VGG-16 [128]. Their 
current state-of-the-art performance for inference tasks 
outperforms 3D diffractive processors. However, unlike 
free-space networks with direct access to the wavefront, 
on-chip processors need extra optoelectronic units for 
capturing and vectorizing visual information.
One critical issue of state-of-the-art photonic chips is 
that they typically require bulky external light sources 
and detectors that lack compactness, but can be 
resolved by emerging integrated coherent sources [129–
131]. Remarkably, emerging optoelectronic materials 
such as perovskites have enabled compact, integrated 
light sources and photodetectors with unprecedented 
efficiency and sensitivity [132]. Their heterogeneous 
integration with optical computing units such as 
MZIs paves the way towards compact, fully on-chip 
optical machine learning platforms. Multiwavelength 
microcomb sources further allow on-chip neural 
networks to perform parallel computation, which 
enhances their processing capacity [133]. Quantum dot 
lasers can also assemble in photonic chips to realize 
reservoir computing, offering another approach for 
compact optical machine learning [134]. This method 
is particularly advantageous for processing time-series 
information from dynamic systems using minimum 
training data and computing resources [135].
3  Tunable materials and reconfigurable photonic 
devices
Artificial intelligence systems fundamentally differ 
from conventional machinery for their adaptability in 
performing diverse complex tasks, thereby requiring 
tremendous 
reconfigurability 
in 
their 
photonic 
components. From operations such as zooming in/
out and focusing in imaging tasks to beamforming in 
telecommunication, tunability are essential for these 
functionalities [136, 137]. Reconfiguration is also 
critical for optical neural networks not only to offer 
re-programmability, but also to accelerate their training 
process via in-situ learning strategies. This section will 
review the materials platforms and device constructions 
for realizing dynamic photonic structures ranging from 
metasurfaces to on-chip units. We will discuss the 
key issues in realizing reconfigurability in intelligent 
photonics and the opportunities in emerging materials/
device systems.
3.1  Materials and device architectures for dynamic 
modulation in free space
Phase change materials represent an important choice to 
achieve dynamic optical responses via temperature change 
or electro-/photo-thermal effects. For example, vana-
dium dioxide ­(VO2) metasurfaces enable dynamic devices 
including perfect absorbers [138] and beam steering [139] 
in infrared and terahertz frequencies via insulator-to-
metal transitions. Nonvolatile materials [140–142] such 
as ­Ge2Sb2Te5 (GST) that switches between amorphous 
and crystalline phases can operate in the infrared–visible 
wavelengths [143–145] (Fig.  5a). A common obstacle for 
these materials is the high temperature needed to trigger 
fast phase transformation, but can be resolved by opti-
mizing the meta-units and electrical pulses for efficient

of amorphous and crystalline phases further enable con-
tinuous, progressive tuning of the optical responses beyond

tunability over the 0-2π phase coverage range, however, is 
still challenging because of the small refractive index con-
trast between the two phases. Another issue of the phase-
change materials is their narrow operation wavelength 
range because the two phases only show distinct optical 
constants in specific parts of the electromagnetic spec-
trum. Also, at least one of the two phases tend to show 
significantly larger optical losses at certain wavelength 
range, thereby preventing the construction of high-effi-
ciency intelligent devices [141]. Therefore, besides efforts 
to improve the integration of phase-change materials at 
device level, materials discoveries are necessary to realize 
low-loss, broadband phase-change materials systems for 
active intelligent photonics [146]. Development of ideal 
phase-change materials for reconfigurable metasurfaces 
is challenging because they need to simultaneously satisfy 
several important properties that are hard observe in a sin-
gle materials platform [147]. Primarily, all materials phases 
need to exhibit broadband transparency with low optical 
losses comparable to ­TiO2 in the visible range to ensure 
the energy efficiency of intelligent photonic devices during 
operation [148]. The ability to trigger phase transformation 
with lower temperature can also make the reconfiguration 
process faster and more energy efficient. To maximize the 
phase coverage within a reasonable device thickness, the 
different phases must exhibit large refractive index contrast 
(Δn > 0.5) and allow continuous tunability of the effective 
index by allowing the presence of mixed materials phases. 
Lastly, the material needs to be compatible with the current 
nanofabrication processes including lithography, deposi-
tion, and etching. Therefore, the discovery of phase-change

3.2  Programmability of on‑chip neural networks
In optical neural networks, the on-chip MZI units 
allow electrical tuning by thermo-optic phase shifters 
[113, 
169] 
that 
modulate 
the 
interference-based 
transformation (Fig.  5d). Therefore, MZIs allow unit-
level programmability over the entire device [98], but 
need correction procedure for the errors induced by 
photodetection and phase encoding units [44]. The 
ability to reconfigure in real-time can combine with 
in-situ learning strategies, which not only accelerate their 
training, but also reduce the errors due to the deviation 
of the experimental device from modeling [85, 170, 171].
Other on-chip units, such as micro-ring resonators, 
also allow dynamic tunability using either phase-change 
or temperature-sensitive materials [172]. For example, 
a reconfigurable optical add-drop multiplexer has been 
demonstrated based on thermal tuning of micro-ring 
resonators to enable arbitrary switching and routing of 
information channels [173]. Thermally tuned phased 
arrays using grating-based antennas further achieves 
tunable beam steering for applications in compact 
light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems [174]. 
Additionally, on-chip optical elements consisting of 
­LiNbO3 [175] enabled diverse tunable electro-optical 
devices ranging from frequency combs [176] to low-
energy photonic switches [177] and phase modulators 
[178, 179] (Fig. 5e). With low optical losses across a broad 
wavelength range of 350–5000  nm [180], this material 
allows dynamic tuning of optical responses because its 
non-centrosymmetric crystal structure enables relative 
displacements of ions under electrical field via Pockels 
effect [181], enabling broad applications including 
high-precision ranging [182], spectroscopy [183, 184], 
and telecommunications [185]. Electrically tunable 
ultrafast on-chip laser sources can also be realized by 
the heterogeneous integration of ­LiNbO3 with ­Si3N4 
waveguides, which further give rise to a compact LiDAR 
device [175]. Lastly, pioneering works on ­LiNbO3-based 
photonic neural networks show great promise for fast, 
energy efficient computing [186, 187].

4  AI for photonics
We envisage that AI technology and photonics will con-
verge in transformative technologies and infrastructures 
to redefine our everyday life. In the vision of metaverse, 
for example, intelligent photonics can provide a high-
throughput, seamless information interface to transmit 
visual content between digital and real worlds within 
systems with extraordinary compactness. The internet of 
things where devices are mutually connected in a high-
speed network can also benefit from this great conver-
gence. The joint advancements of nanophotonics and AI 
exhibit tremendous implications for futuristic medical 
systems that target early and intelligent diagnosis.

Glasses-free 3D displays are also important for AR/VR 
technology [195–198] not only because the elimination 
of glasses/headsets reduces discomforts, but also for its 
ability to deliver large interactive 3D scenes to multiple 
users. Their realization is significantly more challenging 
because the planar screen must display seamlessly to a 
broad range of viewing angles, simultaneously requiring 
a high angular resolution, a wide 3D viewing angle, and 
a high resolution per view [199]. For any 3D display 
techniques to satisfy the above demands, their optical 
modulator components must have a large number of 
degrees-of-freedom to deliver rich visual information 
from 3D scenes to all views. Therefore, current 
commercial demonstrations (e.g. VSTAR Technology 
CO., Ltd. [200] and Ledman Optoelectronic Co., Ltd 
[201].) using conventional bulk optics are typically 
massive in scale, limiting their applications to large 
billboards and outdoor screens. Ongoing miniaturization 
towards tabletop technology (e.g. Looking Glass [202] 
and SVG Tech Group [203]) requires significant size 
reductions for the optical components [196, 204]. 
Nanophotonics can tackle these issues with their unique 
capabilities in subwavelength wavefront modulation 
but need tremendous optimization in their large-scale 
fabrication to lower the device cost. To become a real-
world technology, their dynamic programmability is a 
pressing challenge to tackle with tremendous materials 
and nanofabrication issues, which have been discussed in 
detail in Sect. 3.1.

In holography-based 3D displays designed by Huygens-

of diffraction elements in real time is still expensive for 
most existing computers [208]. ANNs can potentially 
overcome this bottleneck by rapidly predicting close 
approximations of holograms [209–211]. One possible 
shortcoming of the deep-learning-based holography 
reconstruction algorithms is their limited generalizability 
to new, unseen scenes that differ considerably from 
the training datasets, causing degradation of display 
quality due to unwanted artifacts. Introduction of 
physics consistencies based on wave propagation and 
spatial frequency can greatly improve the generalization 
capabilities of the holography models [212, 213]. Other 
branches of 3D display technology also suffer from 
aberrations [214] and visual discomforts [215] that can 
be compensated using ANNs that learn the physical 
causes of aberrations. Metasurface-based optical neural 
networks are also promising platforms for learning-based 
wavefront modulation to achieve seamless, aberration-
free delivery of 3D visual content while greatly improving 
the computing speed. Their design has been a challenge 
due to the lack of effective training framework for 3D 
display tasks that typically require generative models. 
Recent breakthroughs in optical generative models 
based on scattering media [216] or diffusion models 
[217] are bringing hope for this convergence, paving 
the way towards next-generation naked-eye 3D display 
technology.
4.2  Internet of things with smart edge devices
Internet of things (IoTs) envisions a network of 
autonomous devices that collaborate with minimal 
human intervention [218]. The intersection between 
nanophotonics and machine learning provides the 
key enabler of this new paradigm, which requires 
(1) continuous sensing on individual machine for 
environmental awareness, requiring an unrealistic 
number of sensors using existing technology [219]; (2) 
fast communication between devices, which form a 
network with a scale that surpass the current internet by 
orders of magnitude [218]; and (3) immediate decision 
making with delicate instructions that is hard for existing 
centralized AI server [218]. These requirements are hard 
to fulfill with existing optical and computing systems 
but create tremendous opportunities for intelligent 
photonics. Unlike traditional sensors that mainly collect 
intensity, nanophotonic devices can access all degrees 
of freedom of photons, including phase, wavelength, 
polarization, and spatio-temporal data. Therefore, jointly 
developed metasurfaces and smart reconstruction 
methods have realized extraordinarily compact imaging 
and sensing devices [27, 220, 221] for collecting accurate 
and comprehensive environmental data. For example, 
Metalenz has been developing polarization-sensitive 
metasurfaces 
with 
structured-illumination 
sources 
to realize miniaturized face recognition module and 
biometric security systems [218]. The synergy between 
nanophotonics and transformer-based models further 
enables broadband hyperspectral imaging with record

Machine-to-machine networks can contribute to 
technologies that have already started to make an impact 
on the market. Among them, autonomous driving has 
been deployed by Apollo [224, 225] and Waymo [226] but 
also raises concerns in reliability and safety. Integration 
of autonomous vehicles into IoT can provide additional 
security to these technologies by extending the sensing 
and decision-making capabilities of an individual 
vehicle beyond their localized hardware via continuous 
information sharing to reduce the risk of accidents [227, 
228]. Despite the challenges in realizing IoT in general, 
developments in AI-equipped electrical vehicles and 
advanced sensing technology are making integration 
into machine-to-machine networks possible. LiDAR 
systems based on metasurfaces [184, 229] (Fig. 6b) and 
integrated photonics [184, 230] hold great advantages 
in speed, compactness, and accuracy. In particular, this 
technology will benefit tremendously from the ability of 
nanophotonic devices to combine diverse functionalities 
ranging from coherent light generation/amplification 
to beam steering and coherent heterodyne detection. 
Pioneering commercialization efforts by Lucidus [231] 
and PIXAPP [232] are advancing these LiDARs towards 
compact, energy-efficient solutions for measuring 
distance and instantaneous velocity, enabling broad 
applications in autonomous vehicles [233] and robotics 
[234]. Other intelligent photonic systems such as the 
metasurface spectrometers [27] that promote faster data 
collection, communication, and in-sensor computation 
can also greatly enhance the overall performance of the 
machine-to-machine networks of vehicles.
Intelligent-photonics-powered IoT systems can also 
have transformative impacts on smart logistics based 
on robots and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV) systems 
[235]. Currently, autonomous delivery robots (such as 
Starship [236] and Coco [217]) are typically deployed 
around regions with simple road conditions such as 
university campuses while requiring human-intervention 
via remote piloting. Their autonomy has been restricted 
by the limited capabilities of conventional sensors 
including multiple cameras, radars and ultrasonic sensors 
and can advance tremendously in compactness and 
multi-dimensional information processing capabilities 
using intelligent photonics. Concurrently, UAV-based 
delivery systems have been established at small scale in 
cities [237, 238] and rural/mountainous regions as a last-
mile delivery option [239] where the aerial environment 
is relatively simple. Because of the growing economic 
activities in the low-altitude airspace [238, 240], however, 
we foresee a significantly heavier aerial traffic of drones in 
cities that will require intensive navigation and planning 
to enhance efficiency and safety [241]. Compared to 
autonomous ground transportation systems, UAVs 
are typically much smaller in size and therefore favor 
compact sensing and computing devices. The ability for 
miniaturized intelligent photonic devices to collect and 
process visual information with low power consumption 
is crucial for achieving effective object recognition to 
avoid collision while maximizing their long-endurance 
capabilities [242]. Besides safety concerns, integration 
with deep-learning-powered nanophotonic devices can 
greatly enrich the functionalities of UAVs that require 
complex imaging and sensing capabilities. For example, 
UAVs equipped with compact hyperspectral imaging 
systems have broad applications in agriculture [243], 
forestry [244], and geological monitoring [245].
4.3  Medical applications of intelligent photonics
Intelligent photonics can revolutionize medical care and 
health systems by providing fast, high-quality services 
to communities that existing medical systems cannot 
reach. Point-of-care tests can reach remote regions 
that lack the resources for early diagnosis of numerous 
diseases that are hard to treat at later stages [246–248]. 
The difficulty of point-of-care diagnosis comes from two 
main aspects: (1) the limited options of assays/tests that 
can be performed by portable devices and (2) the lack of 
professionally trained personnels to perform the test and 
to analyze the results. Nanophotonics has tremendous 
potential in tackling the first challenge with their ability 
to realize versatile diagnosis in miniaturized systems 
[249–251] such as smartphones [252–254]. Metasurfaces 
with unique imaging [255, 256] and spectral [257–259] 
responses can further reduce the size of the essential 
components for diagnosis systems to micro-meter scale 
[260]. AI technology, on the other hand, is transforming 
how medical data is processed to produce accurate 
test results with minimal human expertise [261–263]. 
Deep learning allows nanophotonic devices to play an 
important role in medical applications such as endo-
microscopy [264], cancer diagnosis [265, 266] as well 
as effective characterization of biomolecules using 
extraordinarily compact designs [267, 268], which was 
impossible for conventional optical systems. For example, 
point-of-care diagnosis systems using flow assays [269, 
270] benefit tremendously from the development of

for point-of-care diagnosis, not only makes it possible 
to perform diagnosis by more powerful AI models, but 
also allows faster responses upon plague outbreaks [279, 
280]. Sensing-communication integration of nanopho-

symptoms such as coughing and their spatial distribu-
tion in the population. By releasing timely alerts, pub-
lic health problems can potentially be avoided, or to the 
least, effectively managed [280]. Data transfer with spe-
cialized medical devices can further predict life-threat-
ening cases such as heart attacks [281, 282] and strokes 
[283, 284], or seek help from emergency medical services 
when the patient losses this capability. To further exploit 
the advantages of intelligent photonics in wearable 
devices, innovations in flexible photonics materials will 
be needed for applications that require conformability to 
the human body. Although there are numerous demon-
strations of flexible photonic devices such as stretchable 
metasurfaces [159, 285, 286], these studies focus on their 
tunability while neglecting the need to maintain deforma-
tion-invariant optical responses, which can be extremely 
challenging for flexible photonic devices but also critical 
for their application in smart wearable devices. For exam-
ple, the imaging and computing properties of existing 
diffractive and metasurface networks are susceptible to 
change if their designs are deformed or stretched, caus-
ing degradation in their performance in sensing and diag-
nosis. Deep-learning-based inverse design frameworks 
can provide effective ways to explore possible designs 
for achieving invariant responses [287]. Overall, the 
innovations on intelligent photonics are promising tech-
nology for achieving better welfare in both smart cities 
and remote areas supported by IoT.
5  Conclusions and outlook
In this review, we have discussed the recent convergence 
of nanophotonics and AI in smart photonic systems. 
Research in intelligent photonics has made substantial 
progress 
in 
the 
past 
decade, 
where 
pioneering 
demonstrations have emerged in diverse applications 
including 
optical 
computing 
and 
reconfigurable 
optoelectronic processing. Nanophotonic structures 
start to revolutionize the hardware for deep-learning 
models towards high-speed, parallel computation at low 
energy consumption. These significant improvements in 
versatility, speed, and compactness compared to existing 
technology can promote grand innovations ranging 
from AR/VR and IoTs to smart health, which require 
the ubiquitous deployment of sensing and computing 
devices. To translate these studies in metasurfaces and 
integrate photonics into real-world innovations, however, 
issues in scalability, programmability, and inference 
accuracy are still prevalent and must be tackled via 
simultaneous breakthroughs in machine-learning theory, 
nanofabrication techniques, and materials systems, 
calling for multi-disciplinary collaborations between 
scientists and engineers from diverse backgrounds. Here 
we give our perspective on these pressing issues:
Scalability and versatility of optical neural networks: 
The performance of photonic neural networks in terms of 
accuracy and generalizability is still limited compared to 
the state-of-the-art AI models so that their advantages in 
speed and power consumption cannot be fully utilized. 
For example, the Taichi chiplets [46] are only comparable 
to the VGG networks [128] which are already superseded 
by more powerful architectures such as transformers 
[12]. So far, efforts to improve the optical networks 
overemphasize on the implementation of nonlinearity 
[92–94] in optical systems to enable, in theory, their 
universal-approximation capabilities [288]. However, 
other mechanisms, such as spatially specific convolution 
operations [8] are crucial but are underexplored. 
In large neural networks, residual connections [11] 
and attention mechanisms [12] are essential for the 
effective training and versatility of these networks. 
All-optical implementation of these mechanisms is 
extremely difficult because of the limitations imposed 
by the physical principles behind light propagation 
and light-matter interactions. Instead, optoelectronic 
computing platforms have significantly large flexibility 
where electronic units can store, replicate, and process 
information with these mechanisms. To realize such 
hybrid AI systems, new theoretical frameworks must be

on physically realizable processes. In particular, the 
architecture consisting of on-chip and free-space optical 
neural networks and integrated electronics should be 
optimized jointly with potential aid from in-situ learning 
techniques and transfer learning strategies that optimize 
the hybrid model in a progressive manner.
Materials systems and nanofabrication methods also 
need to evolve beyond current planar paradigms to 
realize scalable production of these optoelectronic chips 
consisting of multi-layered photonic heterostructures. 
In particular, although diffractive optical networks can 
be fabricated by two-photon 3D printing [289, 290], 
effective management of residual stresses is still needed 
to avoid unwanted warpage and deformation of the 
parts after fabrication [291]. The long-term stability and 
robustness of the nanostructures consisting of polymeric 
materials also need to be tested under device operation, 
which can involve cycles of heating and cooling that 
cause materials fatigue. Although 3D printing of silica has 
been realized at nanoscale resolution [292], the limited 
throughput of these methods prohibits their usage for 
large-scale production processes. Therefore, nanoscale 
3D fabrication methods that can create multi-layered 
low-loss inorganic materials over wafer scale are still 
needed. The fabrication of metasurface neural networks, 
in contrast, potentially allows scalable production 
[293] of each single layer via cost-effective lithography-
based methods, but needs to develop transparent filler/
supporting materials between the layers. Preliminary 
demonstrations of aligned multi-layered metasurface 
devices have been realized using spin-coated photoresist 
materials with high transparency [294]. The transparent 
spacing films created by spin coating, however, can 
suffer from defects due to numerous factors such as 
the unsteady drainage of solvents and imperfect gas 
conditions [295], thereby preventing further fabrication 
steps on top of these spacer layers. Also, photoresists 
such as SU-8 have limited thermal stability and can be 
incompatible with high-temperature semiconductor 
processes that are essential for making other components 
of the AI processor. Inorganic dielectric materials 
such as silica represent another alternative for spacer 
materials, but the thick films are typically produced by 
high-temperature processes such as plasma-enhanced 
chemical vapor deposition and are susceptible to cracking 
due to the stress accumulated during the materials 
cooling [296]. Therefore, low-temperature deposition 
methods of high-quality inorganic materials with low 
refractive index are needed for intelligent photonics.
Error correction in intelligent photonic devices: 
Nanophotonic devices often suffer from errors [44, 83, 
165] due to the imperfections in fabrication as well as the 
limitations of the physical models used in their design. 
Although AI systems can tolerate moderate errors in tasks 
such as inference [162], the errors from a single optical 
unit accumulate exponentially with increasing number 
of neurons [297] and are therefore nontrivial issues for 
building large-scale models. This issue is more prominent 
for intelligent photonics in high-resolution imaging 
and 3D display technology where the user experience 
is extremely sensitive to the discomforts caused by 
deviations of the presented visual information from the 
ground truth [196, 209]. As analog systems, metasurfaces 
and integrated photonics cannot increase their precision 
in the same strategy as digital systems, i.e. by simply 
using more digits to represent the same information 
[162]. Instead, improvements in accuracy must be 
realized by the continuous effort on the optimizations of 
fabrication techniques for analog devices so that drastic 
improvements are often unrealistic in a short period 
[298]. Onsite in-situ learning approaches are promising 
strategies to realize accurate experimental optical systems 
for optical computing and information processing 
[83, 85, 171]. These systems typically consist of (1) 
dynamic optical layers such as spatial light modulators, 
(2) sensors for measuring the network output used to 
quantify the errors, and (3) a digital processor to perform 
backpropagation of errors to update the configuration 
of the active layers. In-situ learning approaches are 
powerful because they provide single-step, systematic 
error correction without tediously modeling each 
possible error sources/mechanisms. However, existing 
demonstrations based on these methods are typically 
task-specific while lacking generalization capabilities 
to new, unseen problems, because the error function 
of each photonic neuron/component is not explicitly 
calibrated. A more universal learning strategy can be 
potentially implemented by a complementary electronic 
neural network that simultaneously learns the errors of 
the neurons/components, which can be reused for error 
corrections in the subsequent training processes for new 
tasks. The realization of a generalizable error-correction 
process will enable accurate intelligent photonics within 
a one-time in-situ learning, holding promises for next-
generation optical computing, imaging, and AR/VR 
systems.

In a longer period beyond 20  years, we are expecting 
novel architectures of optoelectronic neural networks 
that enable versatile sensing-computing tasks, offering 
endless possibilities for smart visual information 
processing in ultra-compact devices. These innovations 
will empower portable edge devices to perform sensing 
and decision-making tasks at an extraordinary efficiency, 
which paves the way to numerous next-generation 
technologies ranging from IoT and metaverse to smart 
health. Commercial realizations of large-scale optical/
optoelectronic neural networks will also provide a high-
speed, energy-efficient solution to centralized computing, 
which gains tremendous significance as the use of large 
AI models becomes prevalent. We expect that multi-
disciplinary collaborations between scientists from broad 
backgrounds will play a key role in these advancements 
in intelligent photonics.

Abstract: The synergistic development of nanophotonics and machine learning has inspired tremendous innovations in both fields in the past decade. In diverse photonics research, deep-learning methods using artificial neural networks become the key game changer that greatly facilitates rapid nanophotonics design and the versatile processing of optical information. Moreover, optical computing platforms that perform calculations through light propagation are receiving tremendous interest as next-generation machine-learning hardware with advantages in computing speed, energy efficiency, and parallelism. This review summarizes the current state-of-the-art nanophotonic devices enabled by machine learning and analyzes the longstanding challenges that must be overcome to make an impact on technology. We also discuss the opportunities of intelligent photonics in applications such as computational imaging/sensing and machine vision. The intersection of nanophotonics with deep learning holds tremendous implications for transformative technologies ranging from internet of things to smart health. Lastly, we provide our perspective on the pressing challenges in intelligent photonics that must be tackled to advance this field to the next level and the vast opportunities for multidisciplinary collaboration.
